However, an earlier independent measurement (Cloudflare blog, using Oct 2022 data) found only ~261 million of ~4 billion Internet users (6.5%) were protected by comprehensive ROV deployment at their access network at that time, with wide regional variance (Sweden and Bolivia >80%; several EU countries and the US just over 50%). [https://nanog.org/stories/articles/rpki-rov-deployment-reaches-major-milestone/ ; https://blog.cloudflare.com/rpki-updates-data/]
effectiveness_verified: mixed — propagation of RPKI-invalid routes declined 24% since early 2022 per Routeviews-based measurement (NANOG/NIST data, May 2024), a reduced-harm trend at the routing-table level; but per-user global protection remained low and geographically very uneven as of the 2022 Cloudflare measurement, and MANRS/Internet Society documented over 3,000 route leaks and hijacks in 2020 alone — the class of incident ROV is meant to prevent. [https://nanog.org/stories/articles/rpki-rov-deployment-reaches-major-milestone/ ; https://blog.cloudflare.com/rpki-updates-data/]

name: DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (TLSA)
public_harm_addressed: fraudulent TLS certificates and CA-based interception
adoption_penetration: Low — a USENIX Security 2020 longitudinal study of 178 million second-level domains across five TLDs (Oct 2017–Oct 2019) found TLSA-record deployment of just 0.65% for .com, 0.73% for .net/.org, 9.8% for .nl, and 38.2% for .se (the outlier, concentrated among a few large hosting/mail providers). [https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec20fall_lee_prepub_0.pdf]
effectiveness_verified: limited — the same study found nearly 36% of deployed TLSA records could not be validated due to missing or incorrect DNSSEC records (18.5% missing DS records in the parent zone; ~14.2% certificate/TLSA mismatches), and among 29 major email providers tested, only 4 supported DANE for both outgoing and incoming mail (two of those with validation deficiencies) — low adoption compounded by high misconfiguration. [https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec20fall_lee_prepub_0.pdf]
source_note: Confirmed RFC 6698 (DANE TLS Protocol: TLSA, Aug 2012) via rfc-editor; binds certificates/keys to DNS names secured by DNSSEC.

name: DNS Certification Authority Authorization Resource Record
public_harm_addressed: unauthorized issuance of certificates for a domain
references_builds_on: DNS; CAA checking mandated by CA/Browser Forum TLS BR (since Sept 2017)
adoption_penetration: ~95,000 base domains CAA-enabled by Nov. 2017 (65k direct + 30k via CNAME), rising from near-zero after CA/Browser Forum Ballot 187 made CAA checking mandatory for CAs on 8 Sept. 2017 (17-1 CA vote, 3-0 browser vote). [https://olivergasser.net/papers/scheitle2018first.pdf ; https://cabforum.org/2017/03/08/ballot-187-make-caa-checking-mandatory/ ; https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8659/]
effectiveness_verified: Mixed — Scheitle et al.'s first empirical audit (ACM SIGCOMM CCR, Vol.48/2, Apr. 2018) found CAA checking exposed real detection value (multiple confirmed mis-issuances leading to revocations) but also found 'at least one CA incorrectly issuing a certificate' in every test performed, i.e., inconsistent CA compliance even after the mandate. [https://olivergasser.net/papers/scheitle2018first.pdf ; https://cabforum.org/2017/03/08/ballot-187-make-caa-checking-mandatory/ ; https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8659/]
source_note: Confirmed RFC 8659 (DNS CAA Resource Record, Nov 2019, obsoletes RFC 6844) via rfc-editor; CAA checking is mandatory for CAs under the CA/B Forum BR.

name: Automatic Certificate Management Environment
public_harm_addressed: error-prone manual domain validation and certificate lapses
references_builds_on: CA/Browser Forum BR domain-control validation; RFC 5280
adoption_penetration: Let's Encrypt (the reference ACME-based CA) issued its 1-billionth certificate in 2020 and was issuing ~10 million certificates/day by late 2025 (first single day over 10M in Sept. 2025); it is, by its own account, the largest CA in the world by certificates issued and is 'closing in on' protecting 1 billion websites (Let's Encrypt 10-Years post, Dec. 2025). [https://letsencrypt.org/2025/12/09/10-years ; https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8555]
effectiveness_verified: Reduced-harm — global share of web page loads over HTTPS rose from below 30% to roughly 80% within five years of Let's Encrypt/ACME's 2015 launch and has held near 80% globally (~95% in the US) since, attributed to ACME's automation removing the manual-issuance barrier to encryption. [https://letsencrypt.org/2025/12/09/10-years ; https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8555]
source_note: Confirmed RFC 8555 (Automatic Certificate Management Environment, March 2019) via rfc-editor; automates domain validation and certificate issuance/renewal (basis of Let's Encrypt).

name: Chrome Root Program Policy
public_harm_addressed: browsers trusting untrustworthy or non-compliant root CAs
references_builds_on: CA/Browser Forum BR; WebTrust/ETSI audits; Common CA Database (CCADB)
adoption_penetration: Current version 1.8, effective 5 Feb. 2026; governs which CA root certificates are trusted by default in Chrome, applying to all CAs seeking or holding inclusion in the Chrome Root Store. [https://googlechrome.github.io/chromerootprogram/ ; https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/root-ca-policy/]
source_note: Confirmed Google's Chrome Root Program Policy (current v1.8, updated 2026-02-05) sets minimum requirements for CA inclusion in Chrome's root store.

name: Mozilla Root Store Policy
public_harm_addressed: software trusting untrustworthy or non-compliant root CAs
references_builds_on: CA/Browser Forum BR; WebTrust/ETSI audits; Common CA Database (CCADB)
adoption_penetration: Version 3.0 effective 15 Mar. 2025 (a further v3.1 update was published by Mozilla Security Blog on 29 June 2026); governs the CA root certificates trusted by default in Firefox and Thunderbird. [https://github.com/mozilla/pkipolicy/blob/master/rootstore/policy.md ; https://blog.mozilla.org/security/2026/06/29/improving-transparency-and-assurance-in-the-web-pki-mozilla-root-store-policy-v3-1/]
source_note: Confirmed Mozilla Root Store Policy current version 3.0 (effective 2025-03-15), maintained via public community consultation; governs CA inclusion in Firefox/Thunderbird.

name: SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange)
public_harm_addressed: undisclosed vulnerable or unlicensed software components
references_builds_on: NTIA SBOM minimum elements; interoperable with CycloneDX and SWID
adoption_penetration: Became ISO/IEC 5962:2021 in Sept. 2021 (Linux Foundation press release), the first open-source SBOM format to reach ISO status; named early adopters include Intel, Microsoft, Siemens, Sony, Synopsys, VMware, and Wind River (the latter reporting 8 years of prior SPDX-format SBOM delivery to customers). A 2024 academic tooling survey (arXiv:2402.11151, Mirakhorli et al.) found SPDX supported by a smaller share of third-party SBOM tools than CycloneDX. [https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/featured/spdx-becomes-internationally-recognized-standard-for-software-bill-of-materials ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11151]
source_note: Linux Foundation press release confirms SPDX approved as ISO/IEC 5962:2021, developed by Linux Foundation, Joint Development Foundation and SPDX community as open SBOM standard.

name: CycloneDX Bill of Materials
public_harm_addressed: unmanaged software/hardware component and vulnerability exposure
references_builds_on: OWASP CycloneDX project; interoperable with SPDX
adoption_penetration: Standardized as Ecma International ECMA-424 on 2 July 2024 (based on CycloneDX v1.6); the 2024 tooling survey (arXiv:2402.11151) found it the most-supported SBOM schema among third-party tools, ahead of SPDX. [https://ecma-international.org/news/ecma-new-standard-ecma-424-on-cyclonedx-bill-of-materials/ ; https://owasp.org/www-project-cyclonedx/]
source_note: Ecma International page confirms ECMA-424 standardizes OWASP CycloneDX (1st ed June 2024, 2nd ed Dec 2025 covering v1.7) under Ecma TC54; JSON BOM for components, services, dependencies, vulnerabilities.

name: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts
owner: Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), Linux Foundation
public_harm_addressed: build-system tampering supply-chain attacks (e.g. SolarWinds-type)
adoption_penetration: Despite growing interest, adoption is 'not widespread' — an empirical study (arXiv:2409.05014, examining 1,523 SLSA-related issues across 233 GitHub repositories, Sept.–Dec. 2024) found complex implementation and unclear communication as the two biggest adoption barriers. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05014 ; https://slsa.dev/blog/2023/05/in-toto-and-slsa ; https://openssf.org/projects/slsa/]
effectiveness_verified: Mixed — the same study concludes some proposed mitigation strategies help, while other adoption challenges 'need future research and tool enhancement,' amid a cited 200% rise in software-supply-chain attacks (Sonatype 2023) motivating SLSA's creation. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05014 ; https://slsa.dev/blog/2023/05/in-toto-and-slsa ; https://openssf.org/projects/slsa/]
source_note: OpenSSF press release and slsa.dev confirm SLSA is an OpenSSF framework; v1.0 released April 2023 (site shows v1.2, 2026 copyright); four build levels of increasing assurance for tamper resistance and provenance.

name: in-toto
owner: Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF); originated NYU Secure Systems Lab
owner_normalised: Cloud Native Computing Foundation ; originated NYU Secure Systems Lab
public_harm_addressed: unauthorized or tampered steps in the software supply chain
references_builds_on: The Update Framework (TUF); integrates with SLSA and OpenVEX
adoption_penetration: Graduated within the CNCF on 23 Apr. 2025 (from Incubating, entered 2022); named production adopters include SolarWinds and Autodesk, and it has been integrated into OpenVEX and the SLSA framework. [https://www.cncf.io/announcements/2025/04/23/cncf-announces-graduation-of-in-toto-security-framework-enhancing-software-supply-chain-integrity-across-industries/]
source_note: CNCF announcement confirms in-toto graduated 23 April 2025, created at NYU (Cappos/Torres-Arias), CNCF-hosted; produces a verifiable record of SDLC steps by authorized entities.

name: NIST Secure Software Development Framework
public_harm_addressed: exploitable software vulnerabilities from insecure development
references_builds_on: OWASP SAMM, BSIMM, SP 800-161; augmented by SP 800-218A (GenAI)
adoption_penetration: Version 1.1 published Feb. 2022. Made mandatory for federal software vendors via OMB Memoranda M-22-18/M-23-16 (self-attestation requirement); this mandate was rescinded on 10 Feb. 2026 by OMB M-26-05, which replaced uniform SSDF self-attestation with agency-discretionary, risk-based vendor validation. [https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/ssdf ; https://www.dwt.com/blogs/privacy--security-law-blog/2026/02/omb-changes-course-on-software-security]
source_note: NIST CSRC SSDF project page confirms SP 800-218 v1.1 with four practice groups (Prepare, Protect, Produce, Respond); final v1.1 dated Feb 2022; SP 800-218A adds a generative-AI community profile.

name: Executive Order 14028, Improving the Nation's Cybersecurity
owner: US Executive Office of the President (White House)
owner_normalised: US Executive Office of the President
public_harm_addressed: supply-chain cyberattacks on government and critical infrastructure
references_builds_on: NIST SSDF; NTIA SBOM minimum elements
adoption_penetration: Signed 12 May 2021, published in the Federal Register 17 May 2021; mandated SBOMs for federal software vendors, secure software development practices, and definition of 'critical software.' Its principal implementation mechanism (OMB-directed SSDF self-attestation) was rescinded and replaced by OMB M-26-05 on 10 Feb. 2026, moving federal agencies to a discretionary, risk-based approach. [https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/05/17/2021-10460/improving-the-nations-cybersecurity ; https://www.dwt.com/blogs/privacy--security-law-blog/2026/02/omb-changes-course-on-software-security]
source_note: Federal Register (86 FR 26633) confirms EO 14028 signed 12 May 2021 by President Biden; mandates SBOMs, secure-software-development attestation, vulnerability scanning, and IoT consumer labeling pilots.

name: Sigstore
owner: Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), Linux Foundation
public_harm_addressed: forged or tampered software artifacts with unverifiable provenance
references_builds_on: X.509, OIDC, Certificate Transparency; adopted by SLSA and package registries
adoption_penetration: Became an OpenSSF Graduated project in Mar. 2024. npm's Sigstore-powered provenance went GA on 3 Oct. 2023; during its public beta (Apr.–Sept. 2023) over 3,800 projects (incl. 134 high-impact ones) adopted build provenance, with over 500 million downloads of provenance-enabled package versions. [https://blog.sigstore.dev/npm-provenance-ga/ ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00271 ; https://blog.sigstore.dev/sigstore-openssf-graduation/ ; https://docs.sigstore.dev/about/security/]
effectiveness_verified: Mixed — a qualitative USENIX Security '25 study (arXiv:2503.00271, 13 practitioner interviews) found keyless/ephemeral signing eased key-management burdens, but enterprise rate-limiting/latency, transparency-log privacy concerns (5 of 6 participants), thin documentation for private deployments, and air-gap incompatibility remain significant adoption barriers. [https://blog.sigstore.dev/npm-provenance-ga/ ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00271 ; https://blog.sigstore.dev/sigstore-openssf-graduation/ ; https://docs.sigstore.dev/about/security/]
source_note: OpenSSF community page confirms Sigstore is an OpenSSF project for signing, verifying and protecting software; components are Cosign (signing), Fulcio (CA), Rekor (transparency log), Gitsign. Founding year not stated on the fetched page, left blank. [Batch year-fill: 2021 (officially launched / first publicly announced), high confidence. https://blog.sigstore.dev/whats-next-for-sigstore-1969e7321f75/]

name: Trusted Platform Module 2.0 Library Specification (ISO/IEC 11889)
public_harm_addressed: platform tampering and unverifiable device integrity
references_builds_on: TCG TPM main specification; Common Criteria TPM protection profiles
adoption_penetration: Standardized internationally as ISO/IEC 11889 (recognized by governments per Microsoft, 2015); Microsoft requires TPM 2.0 as a baseline hardware requirement for Windows 11, driving near-universal presence in new PCs. [https://crocs.fi.muni.cz/_media/publications/pdf/2024-ches-tpmscan.pdf ; https://trustedcomputinggroup.org/resource/tpm-library-specification/]
effectiveness_verified: Limited — TPMScan (CHES 2024 / IACR TCHES), a wide-scale study of 78 TPM firmware versions across 6 vendors (Infineon, Nuvoton, STMicroelectronics, AMD, Microsoft, Intel) over 7 years, found serious vulnerabilities (e.g., new ECC nonce-leakage bugs, one allowing private-key extraction from just nine signatures) persisting despite Common Criteria EAL4+ certification, plus inconsistent vendor vulnerability disclosure/mitigation. [https://crocs.fi.muni.cz/_media/publications/pdf/2024-ches-tpmscan.pdf ; https://trustedcomputinggroup.org/resource/tpm-library-specification/]
source_note: TCG resource page confirms TPM 2.0 Library Specification (latest Rev 185, March 2026, four parts) standardized internationally as ISO/IEC 11889:2015; hardware root of trust for platform integrity and attestation.

name: Device Identifier Composition Engine
public_harm_addressed: unprotected identity and integrity on resource-constrained IoT devices
references_builds_on: TCG; complements TPM; DICE X.509 certificate profiles
adoption_penetration: Adopted into Android via the Open DICE project (Android Open Source Project), used for firmware-stage identity/attestation on Android devices as a lightweight alternative where a full TPM is impractical. [https://source.android.com/docs/security/features/dice ; https://trustedcomputinggroup.org/what-is-a-device-identifier-composition-engine-dice/]
source_note: TCG page confirms DICE is a TCG-published hardware root of trust for devices where a TPM is impractical; provides device identity, measurement and attestation. Specific spec year not stated on fetched page, left blank. [Batch year-fill: 2017 (TCG official announcement of the DICE Architecture specification release), high confidence. https://trustedcomputinggroup.org/tcg-announces-dice-architecture-security-privacy-iot-embedded-devices/]

name: Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) Architecture
public_harm_addressed: relying on an untrustworthy device operating state
references_builds_on: TCG attestation, TPM; underpins EAT and CoRIM formats
adoption_penetration: No published figure identified (checked)

name: FIDO Metadata Service
public_harm_addressed: fraudulent or uncertified authenticators undermining authentication
adoption_penetration: MDS underpins authenticator trust validation across the broader FIDO2/passkey ecosystem, which the FIDO Alliance reports reached roughly 5 billion passkeys in active use worldwide as of its May 2026 World Passkey Day report (90% global awareness, 75% of people having activated at least one passkey). [https://fidoalliance.org/specs/mds/fido-metadata-service-v3.1-ps-20250521.html ; https://fidoalliance.org/five-billion-passkeys-a-milestone-not-a-finish-line/]
source_note: FIDO Alliance page confirms MDS (current MDS3) is a global registry distributing a signed Metadata BLOB used by relying parties to validate authenticator attestation and FIDO Certified status; spec v3.1 dated 2025-05-21.

name: GSMA eSIM Remote SIM Provisioning (SGP.22 Consumer / SGP.32 IoT)
public_harm_addressed: unauthorized SIM provisioning and untrusted device/network access

adoption_penetration: GSMA Intelligence estimates ~850 million eSIM smartphone connections globally in 2025, forecast to reach 6.7 billion (76% of all smartphone connections) by 2030; separately, over 260 mobile operators (MNOs/MVNOs) had already launched commercial eSIM smartphone services as of June 2022. [https://www.gsmaintelligence.com/research/esim-market-progress-consumer-behaviour-and-adoption-to-2030]
source_note: GSMA official documents confirm SGP.32 eSIM IoT Technical Specification v1.0 (May 2023) and SGP.22 Consumer RSP (latest v3.1); GSMA-published eUICC remote provisioning with certificate-based trust chain.

public_harm_addressed: compromised or counterfeit ICT components in the supply chain
references_builds_on: SP 800-53 controls; SP 800-37 Risk Management Framework
adoption_penetration: No published figure identified (checked)

name: Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines

references_builds_on: SP 800-147 (BIOS protection), SP 800-155; roots of trust
adoption_penetration: No published figure identified (checked)

name: OpenSSF Scorecard
owner: Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), Linux Foundation
public_harm_addressed: insecure or unmaintained open-source dependencies
references_builds_on: OpenSSF Best Practices; complements SBOM and dependency scanning
adoption_penetration: Project repository states Scorecard runs a weekly automated scan of the 1 million most critical open-source projects (ranked by OpenSSF Criticality Score); notable listed users include TensorFlow, Angular, Flutter and deps.dev. A 2022 peer-reviewed measurement applied Scorecard to 832,422 of 947,936 npm packages and 191,483 of 211,088 PyPI packages that had GitHub repos. [https://github.com/ossf/scorecard ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03412]
effectiveness_verified: mixed - a 2022 OpenSSF-affiliated peer-reviewed study (ESEM) found substantial real-world gaps in the practices Scorecard checks (Token-Permission, License, Code-Review, Maintained, Branch-Protection, Security-Policy) across both the npm and PyPI ecosystems, concluding several checks need broader industry consensus before they reliably predict security outcomes. [https://github.com/ossf/scorecard ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03412]
source_note: OpenSSF project page confirms Scorecard launched Nov 2020, an OpenSSF Best Practices WG project running automated security-health checks on open-source projects.

name: The Minimum Elements For a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)

adoption_penetration: A Linux Foundation/OpenSSF/SPDX/OpenChain survey of 412 organizations (Q3 2021, published alongside NTIA's report) found 47% were already producing or consuming SBOMs, with 78% expecting to do so by 2022, and 82% familiar with the term SBOM. [https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/press-release/the-linux-foundation-releases-the-state-of-software-bill-of-materials-sbom-and-cybersecurity-readiness-research]

name: Convention Abolishing the Requirement of Legalisation for Foreign Public Documents (Apostille Convention)
owner: Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH)
owner_normalised: Hague Conference on Private International Law
public_harm_addressed: cross-border document fraud; non-recognition of official public documents
adoption_penetration: 130 Contracting Parties as of the HCCH's status table (last updated 30 June 2026). [https://www.hcch.net/en/instruments/conventions/status-table/?cid=41]
effectiveness_verified: limited: HCCH (official): the Convention abolishes multi-step consular legalization, replacing an 'often long and costly legalisation process' with a single Apostille certificate (130 contracting parties; several million Apostilles/year); the e-APP e-Register enables electronic issuance and online verification to counter forged certificates. Direction: the mechanism plausibly reduces authentication steps, time, and cost and enables fraud verification — but the official materials provide NO quantified data on fraud-rate or cost reductions, and rigorous peer-reviewed outcome studies are scarce. Effect direction likely positive; magnitude unquantified.
source_note: WebFetched HCCH Apostille Section: official title 'Convention of 5 October 1961...', 130 Contracting Parties, HCCH as administering body/depositary.

effectiveness_verified: mixed - A peer-reviewed review of comparative field studies (Reganold, 'Soil quality and profitability of biodynamic and conventional farming systems') found biodynamic (Demeter) farms consistently show better soil quality (organic matter, microbial activity, earthworm populations) than conventional farms, but 10-30% lower crop yields; profitability is roughly equal to or better than conventional only when biodynamic products earn 15-108% price premiums - without those premiums net returns run 0-20% lower. [https://demeter.net/about/organisation/]

name: WRAP Certification (12 Principles)

public_harm_addressed: sweatshop labour abuses and unlawful production

[https://mhssn.igc.org/Terwindt-%20CSR%20-International%20Labour%20Review.pdf]

name: MSCI ESG Ratings
public_harm_addressed: greenwashing / mispriced ESG risk

adoption_penetration: Covers more than 17,000 issuers and 999,000 securities worldwide (as of June 30, 2024); MSCI's ESG ratings program was established in 1999, with a continuous time series since 2007. [https://www.msci.com/data-and-analytics/sustainability-solutions/esg-ratings]
effectiveness_verified: Mixed: the peer-reviewed "Aggregate Confusion" study (Berg, Kölbel & Rigobon, Review of Finance, 2022) compared MSCI against five other major ESG raters and found only a 0.61 average pairwise correlation among them (vs. 0.92 for credit ratings from Moody's/S&P), attributing the divergence to differences in measurement (56%), scope (38%) and weighting (6%). [https://www.msci.com/data-and-analytics/sustainability-solutions/esg-ratings]

These are modeled/projected estimates rather than realized ex-post outcomes. [https://tfadatabase.org/en/implementation]

FCC's Dec 19, 2025 Triennial Report on the Efficacy of Call-Authentication Technologies concluded STIR/SHAKEN 'effectively authenticates caller ID information' when correctly implemented, but flagged major real-world gaps: only 4.2% fewer robocalls in 2024 vs. 2023 and a 22% drop in scam calls (modest), alongside a 68% decline in FTC robocall complaints FY2021-2024 (3.4M to 1.1M) attributable to the broader anti-robocall campaign; however honeypot/production data showed scam calls received 'A-level' (highest trust) attestation over 50% of the time and 43% of spam traffic carried A-level signatures, undermining the framework's value. The FCC explicitly stated STIR/SHAKEN is 'not a silver bullet.' TNS's 2022 Robocall Report similarly found only an 8% robocall volume decline (37.9B to 34.9B calls in H1 2022) despite carrier-side adoption, as bad actors shifted to smaller/alternative networks. [https://codata.org/initiatives/data-science-and-stewardship/fundamental-physical-constants/redefinition-of-the-international-system-of-units-si-based-on-the-codata-fundamental-constant/]

name: Multilateral arms-control treaty verification regimes (IAEA nuclear safeguards, OPCW, CTBTO)
owner: International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA); Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW); CTBTO Preparatory Commission
owner_normalised: International Atomic Energy Agency ; Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons ; CTBTO Preparatory Commission
public_harm_addressed: undetected treaty violations and weapons proliferation
references_builds_on: NPT (1968); Chemical Weapons Convention (1993); CTBT (1996); IAEA Statute Art. III
adoption_penetration: IAEA: safeguards agreements in force for 190 States (2025 Safeguards Implementation Report, IAEA Board of Governors, mid-2026). OPCW: 193 States Parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention, covering ~98% of the world's population (opcw.org, as of Dec 2025). CTBTO: 188 signatory states and 179 ratifications of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (ctbto.org), still short of the specific ratifications needed for entry into force. [https://www.opcw.org/media-centre/opcw-numbers; https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/news/iaea-draws-safeguards-conclusions-for-179-states-iaea-report; https://www.ctbto.org/our-mission/states-signatories]
effectiveness_verified: reduced-harm — OPCW: 100% of declared chemical-weapons stockpiles (72,304 metric tonnes) verified as destroyed as of 31 Dec 2025, backed by 2,062+ inspections of destruction facilities since 1997. IAEA: the 'broader conclusion' (all nuclear material remained in peaceful use) was reached for 75 of 190 States in the 2025 report, with safeguards conclusions drawn for 179 of 190 States overall, based on nearly 3,000 in-field verification activities. CTBTO: the International Monitoring System independently detected North Korea's announced nuclear tests (e.g., data on the Feb 2013 test reached member states in about an hour, ahead of DPRK's own announcement), demonstrating verification effectiveness even though the Treaty has not yet formally entered into force. [https://www.opcw.org/media-centre/opcw-numbers; https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/news/iaea-draws-safeguards-conclusions-for-179-states-iaea-report; https://www.ctbto.org/our-mission/states-signatories]
source_note: Confirmed on iaea.org that IAEA safeguards are legally binding agreements under the NPT and that the IAEA administers verification per Art. III of its Statute; OPCW and CTBTO PrepCom run the parallel chemical and nuclear-test verification regimes (official pages seen this session).

name: Wolfsberg Financial Crime Principles for Correspondent Banking
public_harm_addressed: money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion through cross-border correspondent banking
adoption_penetration: The Wolfsberg Group was founded in 2000 by 13 global banks. Its Correspondent Banking Due Diligence Questionnaire (CBDDQ, which operationalizes the CB Principles) was formally welcomed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, CPMI, FATF and the Financial Stability Board in a joint March 2018 statement, and is described by the Basel Institute on Governance as the 'de facto industry standard' for correspondent-banking due diligence. [https://bis.org/press/p180306a.htm; https://baselgovernance.org/blog/collective-action-banking-wolfsberg-groups-role-fast-evolving-industry]
effectiveness_verified: limited/mixed — in that same 2018 statement, the BCBS cautioned the questionnaire should be used only 'as a starting point for the risk assessment,' not a substitute for it; the FSB has separately documented that fixed KYC/due-diligence costs continued to drive roughly one-fifth of correspondent-banking relationship terminations even after the Principles/CBDDQ were in wide use, i.e. adoption of the standard has not eliminated the de-risking problem it targets. [https://bis.org/press/p180306a.htm; https://baselgovernance.org/blog/collective-action-banking-wolfsberg-groups-role-fast-evolving-industry]

adoption_penetration: 160 data repositories worldwide currently hold CoreTrustSeal certification — the certification scheme that most closely operationalizes trustworthy-repository criteria aligned with TRUST — per coretrustseal.org (figure is for the related CoreTrustSeal network, not a direct TRUST-principles adoption count). [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-020-0486-7]
source_note: Nature Scientific Data 7:144, published 14 May 2020, led by Dawei Lin (19 authors); TRUST = Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, Technology.

name: ARRIVE Guidelines 2.0 (Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments)
owner: NC3Rs (National Centre for the Replacement, Refinement and Reduction of Animals in Research)
public_harm_addressed: irreproducible, poorly reported animal research; wasted resources and animals
adoption_penetration: No published figure identified (checked)
effectiveness_verified: A cross-sectional analysis of 943 published animal studies found reporting quality significantly improved across three periods: pre-ARRIVE 1.0 (2005–2010, 53.95% rated 'average' or better), post-ARRIVE 1.0 (2014–2019, 73.94%), and post-ARRIVE 2.0 (2021, 90.20%; p<0.001) — but zero of the 943 studies fully reported all 38 ARRIVE items, indicating a positive-but-incomplete ('mixed') effectiveness verdict. [https://cdt.amegroups.org/article/view/132375/html]
source_note: PLOS Biology, published 14 July 2020 (pbio.3000410); NC3Rs; Essential 10 + Recommended Set checklist updating the original 2010 ARRIVE guidelines. Confirms candidate's 2020 date.

public_harm_addressed: legal uncertainty and disputes in cross-border trade finance

adoption_penetration: UNCITRAL (UN Commission on International Trade Law) formally endorsed URF 800 at its 50th plenary session, Vienna, 14 July 2017 — the first global standardized rules for forfaiting, per ICC's own announcement. [https://iccwbo.org/news-publications/news/un-endorses-icc-uniform-rules-forfaiting-urf-800/]

name: Proprietary Fingerprint Template Evaluation (PFT III)
owner: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), ITL Image / Biometric Technologies Group
public_harm_addressed: inaccurate fingerprint matching causing false identification
adoption_penetration: 60 template submissions from approximately 30 vendors across multiple countries (US, China, Lithuania, Germany, France, Japan, and others), per NIST's PFT III results page. [https://pages.nist.gov/pft/results/pftiii/]
source_note: Confirmed on nist.gov: PFT III is NIST's ongoing one-to-one proprietary fingerprint template matching evaluation (succeeded PFT II 2010-2019, original PFT 2003-2010); run by NIST ITL.

name: Slap Fingerprint Segmentation Evaluation (SlapSeg)
owner: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), ITL Biometric Technologies Group
public_harm_addressed: poor slap-print segmentation degrading downstream fingerprint matching
adoption_penetration: 17 vendor/algorithm submissions in SlapSegII (2009); ~10-12 active vendor submissions (IDEMIA, NEC, Thales, DERMALOG, Neurotechnology, Innovatrics, ROC, Rank One Computing, etc.) in the ongoing SlapSeg III cycle, with active entries dated 2022-2025 [https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=901467]
effectiveness_verified: mixed - NISTIR 7553 (Jan 2009) found leading algorithms segmented 94-99% of four-finger slap images correctly (96-99% for 'any 3 fingers' on 3-inch slaps; 94-97% for all 5 finger positions among top performers), but accuracy varied widely across the 17 participants and thumb segmentation remained a persistent weak point across nearly all algorithms [https://tsapps.nist.gov/publication/get_pdf.cfm?pub_id=901467]
source_note: Confirmed on nist.gov: SlapSeg (SlapSeg04 first; SlapSegII/III ongoing) evaluates slap-fingerprint segmentation algorithms against reference data; run by NIST ITL.

name: Evaluation of Latent Fingerprint Technologies (ELFT)
owner: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), ITL Image Group
public_harm_addressed: inaccurate latent (forensic) fingerprint matching causing wrongful identification
adoption_penetration: 5 commercial AFIS vendors (Sagem, NEC, Cogent, Sonda, Warwick) in ELFT-EFS Evaluation #1, completed March 2011, searching 1,114 latents from 837 subjects against 100,000 exemplars; grown to 22 participating vendors in the current 2026 evaluation cycle against FBI and DoD datasets [https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/IR/nistir7775.pdf]
effectiveness_verified: mixed - NISTIR 7775 (ELFT-EFS Eval #1, 2011) explicitly states 'the effect of the use of EFS features other than minutiae was mixed,' with rank-1 identification rates of 40.6-59.4% for image-only search vs. 47.2-62.9% for image+full Extended Feature Set search (24.2-43.9% for minutiae-only), and the report noting the latent image itself was the single most effective search component; NISTIR 7859 (Eval #2, 2012) found improvements in most cases but characterized results only as 'promising,' recommending further study [https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/IR/nistir7775.pdf]
source_note: Confirmed on nist.gov: ELFT is NIST's ongoing evaluation of latent (forensic) fingerprint matching technologies (ELFT 07 first; ELFT-EFS evaluations); run by NIST ITL Image Group.
